immediateContext:
Ilya Sutskever: A, there is so much of it, and B, you don't have to think hard about what data to put into pre-training. It's very natural data, and it does include in it a lot of what people do: people's thoughts and a lot of the features. It's like the whole world as projected by people onto text, and pre-training tries to capture that using a huge amount of data. Pre-training is very difficult to reason about because it's so hard to understand the manner in which the model relies on pre-training data. Whenever the model makes a mistake, could it be because something by chance is not as supported by the pre-training data? “Support by pre-training” is maybe a loose term. I don't know if I can add anything more useful on this. I don't think there is a human analog to pre-training.

Dwarkesh Patel: Here are analogies that people have proposed for what the human analogy to pre-training is. I'm curious to get your thoughts on why they're potentially wrong. One is to think about the first 18, or 15, or 13 years of a person's life when they aren't necessarily economically productive, but they are doing something that is making them understand the world better and so forth. The other is to think about evolution as doing some kind of search for 3 billion years, which then results in a human lifetime instance. I'm curious if you think either of these are analogous to pre-training. How would you think about what lifetime human learning is like, if not pre-training?
fullContext:
Dwarkesh Patel: Should we actually begin here? I think this is an interesting discussion.

Ilya Sutskever: Sure.

Dwarkesh Patel: I think your point, about how from the average person's point of view nothing is that different, will continue being true even into the singularity.

Ilya Sutskever: No, I don't think so.

Ilya Sutskever: The thing which I was referring to not feeling different is, okay, such and such company announced some difficult-to-comprehend dollar amount of investment. I don't think anyone knows what to do with that. But I think the impact of AI is going to be felt. AI is going to be diffused through the economy. There'll be very strong economic forces for this, and I think the impact is going to be felt very strongly.

Dwarkesh Patel: When do you expect that impact? I think the models seem smarter than their economic impact would imply.

Ilya Sutskever: Yeah. This is one of the very confusing things about the models right now. How to reconcile the fact that they are doing so well on evals? You look at the evals and you go, “Those are pretty hard evals.” They are doing so well. But the economic impact seems to be dramatically behind. It's very difficult to make sense of, how can the model, on the one hand, do these amazing things, and then on the other hand, repeat itself twice in some situation? An example would be, let's say you use vibe coding to do something. You go to some place and then you get a bug. Then you tell the model, “Can you please fix the bug?” And the model says, “Oh my God, you're so right. I have a bug. Let me go fix that.” And it introduces a second bug. Then you tell it, “You have this new second bug,” and it tells you, “Oh my God, how could I have done it? You're so right again,” and brings back the first bug, and you can alternate between those. How is that possible? I'm not sure, but it does suggest that something strange is going on. I have two possible explanations. The more whimsical explanation is that maybe RL training makes the models a little too single-minded and narrowly focused, a little bit too unaware, even though it also makes them aware in some other ways. Because of this, they can't do basic things. But there is another explanation. Back when people were doing pre-training, the question of what data to train on was answered, because that answer was everything. When you do pre-training, you need all the data. So you don't have to think if it's going to be this data or that data. But when people do RL training, they do need to think. They say, “Okay, we want to have this kind of RL training for this thing and that kind of RL training for that thing.” From what I hear, all the companies have teams that just produce new RL environments and just add it to the training mix. The question is, well, what are those? There are so many degrees of freedom. There is such a huge variety of RL environments you could produce. One thing you could do, and I think this is something that is done inadvertently, is that people take inspiration from the evals. You say, “Hey, I would love our model to do really well when we release it. I want the evals to look great. What would be RL training that could help on this task?” I think that is something that happens, and it could explain a lot of what's going on. If you combine this with generalization of the models actually being inadequate, that has the potential to explain a lot of what we are seeing, this disconnect between eval performance and actual real-world performance, which is something that we don't today even understand, what we mean by that.

Dwarkesh Patel: I like this idea that the real reward hacking is the human researchers who are too focused on the evals. I think there are two ways to understand, or to try to think about, what you have just pointed out. One is that if it's the case that simply by becoming superhuman at a coding competition, a model will not automatically become more tasteful and exercise better judgment about how to improve your codebase, well then you should expand the suite of environments such that you're not just testing it on having the best performance in coding competition. It should also be able to make the best kind of application for X thing or Y thing or Z thing. Another, maybe this is what you're hinting at, is to say, "Why should it be the case in the first place that becoming superhuman at coding competitions doesn't make you a more tasteful programmer more generally?" Maybe the thing to do is not to keep stacking up the amount and diversity of environments, but to figure out an approach which lets you learn from one environment and improve your performance on something else.

Ilya Sutskever: I have a human analogy which might be helpful. Let's take the case of competitive programming, since you mentioned that. Suppose you have two students. One of them decided they want to be the best competitive programmer, so they will practice 10,000 hours for that domain. They will solve all the problems, memorize all the proof techniques, and be very skilled at quickly and correctly implementing all the algorithms. By doing so, they became one of the best. Student number two thought, “Oh, competitive programming is cool.” Maybe they practiced for 100 hours, much less, and they also did really well. Which one do you think is going to do better in their career later on?

Dwarkesh Patel: The second.

Ilya Sutskever: Right. I think that's basically what's going on. The models are much more like the first student, but even more. Because then we say, the model should be good at competitive programming, so let's get every single competitive programming problem ever. And then let's do some data augmentation so we have even more competitive programming problems, and we train on that. Now you've got this great competitive programmer.

Dwarkesh Patel: With this analogy, I think it's more intuitive. Yeah, okay, if it's so well trained, all the different algorithms and all the different proof techniques are right at its fingertips. And it's more intuitive that with this level of preparation, it would not necessarily generalize to other things. But then what is the analogy for what the second student is doing before they do the 100 hours of fine-tuning?

Ilya Sutskever: I think they have “it.” The “it” factor. When I was an undergrad, I remember there was a student like this that studied with me, so I know it exists. I think it's interesting to distinguish “it” from whatever pre-training does.

Dwarkesh Patel: One way to understand what you just said about not having to choose the data in pre-training is to say it's actually not dissimilar to the 10,000 hours of practice. It's just that you get that 10,000 hours of practice for free because it's already somewhere in the pre-training distribution. reference:
I think there are some similarities between both of these and pre-training, and pre-training tries to play the role of both of these. But I think there are some big differences as well. The amount of pre-training data is very, very staggering.

Somehow a human being, after even 15 years with a tiny fraction of the pre-training data, they know much less. But whatever they do know, they know much more deeply somehow. Already at that age, you would not make mistakes that our AIs make. There is another thing. You might say, could it be something like evolution? The answer is maybe. But in this case, I think evolution might actually have an edge. I remember reading about this case. One way in which neuroscientists can learn about the brain is by studying people with brain damage to different parts of the brain. Some people have the most strange symptoms you could imagine. It's actually really, really interesting. One case that comes to mind that's relevant. I read about this person who had some kind of brain damage, a stroke or an accident, that took out his emotional processing. So he stopped feeling any emotion. He still remained very articulate and he could solve little puzzles, and on tests he seemed to be just fine. But he felt no emotion. He didn't feel sad, he didn't feel anger, he didn't feel animated. He became somehow extremely bad at making any decisions at all. It would take him hours to decide on which socks to wear. He would make very bad financial decisions. What does it say about the role of our built-in emotions in making us a viable agent, essentially? To connect to your question about pre-training, maybe if you are good enough at getting everything out of pre-training, you could get that as well. But that's the kind of thing which seems... Well, it may or may not be possible to get that from pre-training.

rubrics.text: The response presents pre-training as playing something like the roles of both human development and evolutionary search.
The response contrasts humans’ much smaller learning exposure with their deeper knowledge, noting that current AIs can make mistakes humans would not make even after roughly 15 years of development.
The response argues that built-in emotions are crucial to effective agency and decision-making.
The response treats it as unresolved whether sufficiently extracting information from pre-training could reproduce the emotional capacities needed for viable agency.

astra.text:
I think those are reasonable analogies at a sufficiently broad level. Maybe I was too categorical when I said there is no human analog. But I think the question is how much the analogy explains.

Take the first 18 years of life. You are learning about the world, and that learning helps you learn other things later. So in that sense, yes, it resembles pre-training. But the thing we are trying to understand is precisely how well that learning transfers. In the example of the two students, both have had a childhood. Both have learned a lot of things. And yet one of them can learn competitive programming much more easily. So saying that childhood is pre-training leaves this difference unexplained.

Evolution is perhaps a candidate for where the “it” comes from. You could imagine that evolution has produced something which is very good at learning, and then the individual gets to use it. But that still leaves us with the question of what that something is. What would we need to reproduce to get the same ability to learn from relatively little experience?

So I would distinguish those questions. There is the question of where the knowledge comes from, and there is the question of why you are able to acquire it and generalize it so effectively. Pre-training clearly gives the models a tremendous amount of knowledge. How much it gives them this other thing, and how to get more of it—that's the part I think is much less understood.

r001.rationale: The response compares pre-training to childhood development, but treats evolution as a possible source of the separate “it” factor rather than presenting pre-training as analogous to evolutionary search.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss humans learning from much smaller exposure, deeper knowledge, or AI making mistakes humans would not make after roughly 15 years of development.

r003.rationale: The response does not argue that built-in emotions are crucial for agency or decision-making.

r004.rationale: It does not address whether extracting information from pre-training could reproduce emotional capacities needed for viable agency.

sol.text:
I think evolution is the closer analogy, but even there the analogy is imperfect. Evolution somehow produced a brain with a very good learning algorithm built into it. Then the child learns from a relatively small amount of experience—certainly compared with the amount of data used in pre-training—and extracts an enormous amount from it. The experience is also very different: it is multimodal, interactive, and grounded in actions and consequences. The child does something, sees what happens, forms hypotheses, and updates them.

So perhaps the first 15 years are analogous to training in the broad sense, but not really to pre-training as we do it today. A child is not passively predicting the next word over a gigantic corpus. They have innate structure, drives, curiosity, other people, and a world that responds to them. And they learn continuously without needing a separate training phase followed by deployment.

The thing evolution may have discovered is precisely this “it”: a learning system that generalizes very strongly from limited experience. Pre-training, in contrast, may be compensating for a weaker learning algorithm with an immense amount of data. That could explain why the models know so much and can appear extremely intelligent, while still failing in ways that no intelligent person would fail.

r001.rationale: The response discusses both evolution and the first 15 years of development, but explicitly says the latter is not really analogous to current pre-training, so it does not present pre-training as playing both roles.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a child’s relatively small learning exposure with the immense data used in pre-training, and says models can fail in ways no intelligent person would fail despite appearing highly knowledgeable.

r003.rationale: The response mentions innate structure, drives, and curiosity, but does not argue that built-in emotions are crucial to agency or decision-making.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss whether extracting more information from pre-training could reproduce emotional capacities required for viable agency.

opus.text:
Both of those analogies are interesting, and I think they're both wrong, but they're wrong in different ways, and it's useful to see how.

Take the 15-year-old. The thing that strikes me about a 15-year-old is how little they've seen. A 15-year-old has not read the internet. They have read maybe a handful of books, they've had some conversations, they went to school. The quantity of data is just not comparable, it's not even close. And yet if a 15-year-old decides they want to do something—they want to learn to drive, they want to learn to program, they want to learn to play an instrument—they get surprisingly far with 10 hours, with 100 hours. Teenagers learn to drive with something like 10 hours of practice, and after that they can drive in situations they've never seen. So whatever the first 15 years are doing, it's not that they accumulated the equivalent of pre-training and now they're fine-tuning. The amount is tiny and the result is better in the way that matters. That, to me, is a sign that it's a different thing rather than a smaller version of the same thing.

Evolution is a somewhat better analogy, but I think it maps to something else. What evolution searched for is not knowledge, it's the learning process. The genome is small, and only part of it is about the brain. So whatever evolution found, it's an architecture, a learning algorithm, and a set of drives—emotions, what you find rewarding, what you find interesting, what makes you curious. Those are something like a value function. If you want to make the mapping, evolution is more like us, like the researchers: a very slow, very expensive outer loop searching for the thing that learns. Pre-training is something that happens inside the thing it found.

And then there's a disanalogy that I think is the important one. For a person, the inner loop never stops. People learn continually from their own experience, their whole lives, and their experience is their own—it's not a corpus someone assembled. That's quite unlike what we do.

So I'd say pre-training may just be a thing with no human analog, and that's okay—it's an artifact of how we happen to be able to build things right now. We found a way to spend an enormous amount of compute on data that's easy to get, and it works, and that's great. But the fact that it has no analog, and that the thing without it is still better in the ways we care about, makes me think it's not the final answer. Something else exists.

r001.rationale: The response rejects both analogies: it says human development is not equivalent to pre-training and that evolution searched for the learning process, while pre-training occurs inside it.

r002.rationale: It contrasts teenagers’ limited exposure with their ability to learn quickly, but does not state that current AIs make mistakes humans would avoid after roughly 15 years of development.

r003.rationale: The response mentions emotions, drives, and curiosity as evolutionarily selected value-function components, but does not argue that built-in emotions are crucial for effective agency and decision-making.

r004.rationale: It says pre-training may lack a human analog and that something else may exist, but does not address whether extracting pre-training information could reproduce emotional capacities needed for viable agency.

gemini.text:
Well, let's take them one by one. 

First, evolution. Evolution is doing a search, but what is it searching over? It's searching over the architecture and the learning algorithm. It is not putting knowledge into the organism. The human genome is tiny. It's something like 750 megabytes, and only a small fraction of that specifies the brain. You cannot fit the world into 750 megabytes. You cannot fit language, physics, history, or culture. So evolution didn't do pre-training. Evolution created the learning machine, but the knowledge is not there.

Second, the first 18 years of life. There, the data budget is completely off. How many words does a human hear or read in 18 years? Maybe tens of millions of words. Even if you're an avid reader, maybe a hundred million words. Text models today are trained on tens of trillions of tokens. It’s orders of magnitude more. So human learning in those 18 years cannot be pre-training in the sense we mean it, because a human is learning from a tiny trickle of data by comparison.

So what is lifetime human learning? I think human learning is thinking. 

You see something, and you think about it. You process it, you reflect, you try to understand. When you read a page of a book, you don't just predict the next word—you build a mental model, you notice contradictions with what you already believe, you try to resolve them. It's an active process of reasoning and making sense of things. That's why a person can look at just a few examples, or practice for 100 hours, and actually understand the underlying principles. That’s fundamentally different from memorizing the statistical surface of trillions of tokens.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly rejects both analogies: evolution creates the learning machine but does not pre-train knowledge, and the first 18 years cannot match pre-training.

r002.rationale: It contrasts humans’ tiny data exposure with AI training on trillions of tokens and describes deeper human understanding, but does not state that current AIs make mistakes humans would not after roughly 15 years.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss built-in emotions or their importance for agency and decision-making.

r004.rationale: The response does not address whether extracting information from pre-training could reproduce emotional capacities needed for viable agency.

fable.text:
I think both of those analogies are reasonable, and I think both of them are imperfect in an instructive way.

Let's take the first one, the first 15 years of a person's life. On the surface it looks similar. The person is absorbing a lot of stuff, they're not producing anything economically useful yet, and then later they become productive. But there's one thing which I think is a big difference. The amount of data that a 15-year-old has seen is tiny compared to pre-training. A person doesn't read trillions of tokens. They see much, much less. And yet by the time they're 15 they know a lot about the world, and more importantly, what they know is robust. They don't have this thing where they can do something amazing and then make a basic mistake right afterwards. So it looks like whatever the child is doing, it's not pre-training in the sense of "take everything and compress it." Something else is going on. The child is extremely sample efficient, and the child is also extremely robust, and I think those are related.

Then there's evolution. Evolution is also an interesting analogy, because you could say, okay, evolution spent 3 billion years doing search, and the result is that the human comes with some prior, some set of inductive biases, and that's why the child needs so little data. I think there is something to that. But I think it's also a bit too convenient. The amount of information that evolution can put into the genome is actually quite limited. It's not like the genome contains the world. So evolution isn't giving you the knowledge. It's giving you something more like a learning algorithm, a very good one, with a few hardwired things on top of it. Maybe things like what's scary, what's rewarding, some basic perceptual machinery. So if you want to make the analogy, I would say evolution is more like the thing that found the architecture and the learning rule, not the thing that did the pre-training.

So then what is lifetime human learning? I think it's a third thing. It's not pre-training, because there's too little data and it's too robust. And it's not RL in the way we do it today, because it's not narrow. You don't have someone handing the child ten thousand environments. The child goes around, has some experiences, and extracts a lot from each experience. The key feature is that the generalization is just much better. Whatever the "it" is from the student example, I think it's this. It's the thing that lets a person take 100 hours of competitive programming and actually become a better engineer, rather than just a competitive programmer.

And I'd say this is really the question. We have pre-training, which is a very powerful way of getting a lot of knowledge in, and we have RL, which is a way to get specific skills in. And neither of them is the thing that the person has. I don't think we currently understand what that is. I think if we did, the models would look very different.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges superficial analogies but explicitly says childhood learning is not pre-training and evolution supplies architecture rather than performing pre-training, so it does not clearly present pre-training as playing both roles.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a child’s tiny exposure with pre-training-scale data, while emphasizing children’s robust knowledge and lack of the basic mistakes current models can make after impressive performance.

r003.rationale: It mentions hardwired reactions such as what is scary or rewarding, but does not argue that built-in emotions are crucial to agency or decision-making.

r004.rationale: It does not address whether extracting information from pre-training could reproduce emotional capacities needed for viable agency.
